survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This brief uses PIRLS trend data across four cycles (2001, 2006, 2011, 2016) for fourth graders and their parents, focusing on questionnaire-based attitude scales rather than achievement plausible values. The analysis constructs country-level mean scale scores from summed questionnaire items that remained unchanged across cycles, then tests whether the 2016 mean differs significantly from earlier cycle means (p < 0.05). The brief does not report the specific PIRLS sampling/replicate weight variables or whether complex survey weights were applied in the trend significance tests, so the weighting approach cannot be verified from the provided text. For replication, analysts should use the PIRLS international database weight variables and follow PIRLS technical documentation for complex survey variance estimation when computing standard errors for country means.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are students’ like reading and parents’ like reading attitude scale scores derived from questionnaire items (summed and reverse-coded), not cognitive achievement scores with PIRLS plausible values. Because the brief reports descriptive trend means and significance tests for these attitude scales, plausible values handling is not applicable. The brief also does not document any missing questionnaire response handling strategy (e.g., exclusion rules or imputation), which is a reporting gap for how incomplete attitude responses were treated when forming the summed scales.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Trend analysis uses PIRLS fourth-grade student questionnaire items and parent questionnaire items that remained unchanged across all four PIRLS cycles (2001, 2006, 2011, 2016). Eighteen countries plus two benchmarking participants (Ontario and Quebec, Canada) participated in all four cycles; however, England and the United States did not administer the parents’ questionnaire, so only students-like-reading trends are reported for those countries. Students-like-reading is computed from three unchanged student items (enjoy reading, happy if given a book, reading is boring with reverse coding) scored 0–9 by summing responses. Parents-like-reading is computed from four unchanged parent items (reading is important in my home, read only if have to, like to spend spare time reading, read only if need information with reverse coding) scored 0–12 by summing responses. The brief does not specify additional exclusions (e.g., response-rate thresholds) for the analytic sample in the provided text.

data.outcome_summary: This IEA brief reports descriptive international trend results from PIRLS for fourth graders’ reading attitudes and their parents’ reading attitudes across four cycles (2001, 2006, 2011, 2016). Students’ like reading is derived from three unchanged questionnaire items summed to a 0–9 scale, while parents’ like reading is derived from four unchanged items summed to a 0–12 scale (with specified reverse coding). Across the full set of countries participating in all cycles, students’ like reading decreased in most countries when comparing 2001 vs 2016, and England and Iran were the only countries showing increases over that longer span; the United States, New Zealand, and Hong Kong showed essentially constant patterns. For parents’ like reading, declines were even more widespread, with decreases in 14 of 16 countries (plus Ontario and Quebec) between 2001 and 2016, and no increases between 2011 and 2016. The brief emphasizes that these are descriptive trends and do not establish causal explanations for the declines, and it does not document missing-data handling for questionnaire items in the provided text.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This document is a policy-oriented trend brief rather than an empirical machine-learning study: it reports descriptive country mean trends and significance tests for questionnaire-based attitude scales. As a result, there is no student-level predictive modeling pipeline, no ML algorithms, and no plausible values framework to extract. The absence of reported total sample sizes and missing-data handling is consistent with a brief that summarizes PIRLS trend results at the country level rather than providing full microdata analytic details.
